cells.tense: The first spark has become a practice you actually keep, and you can feel it happening now.
cells.ask: Notice when a session takes hold without strain, and stop while it is still easy to start again tomorrow.
cells.core:
You said you would practice, and you do — a little each day, whether or not it feels like much. What you tend has outlasted the first enthusiasm, which is quieter and rarer than people expect.

The sign it is going well is simple: the repetition has stopped being something you negotiate. Starting is easy, sessions end while one more is still possible, and you leave wanting tomorrow. That is what feeds what comes after. Lately it may have stopped producing anything visible — the work is real, it just doesn't announce itself. Set down the need to see what it's doing. Notice when a session takes hold without strain, and stop while it is still easy to pick up again. The cost is a little of the satisfaction of proving you did enough today.
cells.sheetLine: You keep a practice going and you can feel the keeping.
cells.verb: to turn a first spark of intention into a settled practice
cells.place: in the room where you practice alone, by repetition, with no audience

cells.tense: You are already living in the day this practice finally arrives, so every session gets graded against it.
cells.ask: Cut the practice to something so small it looks almost pointless, and do only that, once, today.
cells.core:
Part of you is already living in the day this pays off. Every session is measured against that day, so nothing you do now counts as complete. You push a little harder each time to close the gap, and the gap keeps feeling wider.

Ease lives on the other side of that pressure. You sit down because the practice is what is true today, not because it promises a result — and the result is doing the sitting. What was a small effort has become a scoreboard, and repetition made of pressure stops being repetition. Cut it down to something so small it looks pointless, and do only that once today. Nothing gets finished that way, but nothing gets pushed forward off its feet either. The rest of you can catch up to the pace you started at.

cells.tense: The practice did not get picked up again, and the door is still standing where you left it.
cells.ask: Do the flat version for ten minutes today, just to show the action still works, and tell one person you did it.
cells.core:
The start has gone quiet. You used to sit down more easily, or you watched yourself about to and then found something else. What stayed is a small wanting to begin again that you keep not acting on. Nothing is spoiled — the spark has just gone unused long enough that starting now feels like more than it is.

In balance, ten minutes counts and nothing has to be proven to anyone. Starting has weight on it now and you are waiting for it to feel light again. It won't feel light first. Do the flat version today, ten minutes, just to show the action still works, and tell one person you did it. That is a beginning you can see from here, and you don't need the old enthusiasm back to take it.

cells.tense: You are already practicing — the sitting down happens, the repetitions happen — you just call it something else.
cells.ask: When the next session is over, say out loud that it was yours, and what it was for.
cells.core:
The practicing is happening already. There is something you do over and over — unhurried, unremarkable, yours — and you would not call it a practice. Meanwhile you talk about the spark as something that might come later, as though you were still waiting for it.

The doing runs on its own; the owning of it doesn't. In balance the practice is simply yours, chosen today because it is the thing in front of you. You don't have to say the word practice or make a plan. When the next session is over, say out loud that it was yours — and what it was for. That sentence is the whole move, and it may be all you need before you do anything else with it.
cells.sheetLine: You are already practicing. You have not said so.

A reader could reasonably say 'I haven't even started one.' The asks survive the miss: starting the flat version and letting one round stand are usable work whether a habit exists yet or not. The draft line that served the writer, 'a small, steady flame,' was cut for image and for flattery.
